blocks.x: Winnipeg's housing starts grew faster than in any other big Canadian city

Winnipeg's housing starts grew faster than those of any other of Canada's 10 largest cities from January to July 2026, the [City of Winnipeg reported on August 20, 2026](https://www.winnipeg.ca/news/2026-08-20-winnipeg-leads-major-canadian-cities-housing-growth). Starts reached 3,514, up 40.4% from a year earlier. Completions rose 52.7% to 2,936 units. Nationally, starts fell about 4.1% over the same period.

The City's figures cover all housing, with no breakdown by tenure. Purpose-built rental supply in the Winnipeg area grew 2.6% in 2025, according to [CMHC's 2025 rental report](https://eppd1strscr01.blob.core.windows.net/cmhcprdcontainer/sf/project/archive/housing_markets/rentalmarketreportcanadaandselectedmarkets/rental-market-report-2025-fall-en.pdf). New rental buildings tend to come with modern windows, new flooring, in-suite laundry and fresh common areas. Renters who used to choose between older buildings will increasingly have new options.
Where older Winnipeg rental buildings feel it first

Older walk-ups and mid-rises are a familiar part of Winnipeg's rental stock. Many are well located and solidly built. But CMHC's 2025 report says vacancy rose most in pre-1960 buildings, as they struggled to compete with newer ones, while buildings from 1975 to 2004 stayed the tightest.
Where an older building falls behind, it tends to be in a few predictable areas:
**Comfort:** drafty single-pane or failing windows, and doors that leak cold air.
**Appearance:** dated hallway carpet, tired paint and worn entrance areas.
**Exterior condition:** spalling brick, cracked parging and stained façades.
**Layout:** small [kitchens](/services/kitchen-renovations) and [bathrooms](/services/bathroom-renovations) that feel cramped next to new open-plan units.

Rent data adds to the picture. [liv.rent's October 2026 report](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631) shows unfurnished one-bedroom asking rents falling for three straight months, though still up 1.7% from a year earlier. When supply rises, older units without upgrades can be among the first to need concessions.
Our view: run renovation like a program, not a series of emergencies

Many older buildings are renovated reactively: a window fails, a tenant complains, a unit turns. The work gets done, but it is scattered, it can cost more per unit, and the building never looks noticeably better.
A planned program works differently. The owner or property manager:
**Assesses the whole building** (envelope, common areas and a sample of units).
**Ranks work by risk and return:** water and envelope first, then common areas, then units.
**Bundles similar work** so one contractor mobilizes once for all the windows, all the hallway flooring or all the masonry.
**Schedules around tenancies** to minimize disruption.
Bundling matters. Mobilizing a crew is a fixed cost; spreading it across a building, rather than one unit at a time, can lower the per-unit cost and produce a visible result tenants notice.

The rules to watch

The 2027 rent guideline in Manitoba is 3%. With the exemption threshold rising to $2,000 in January 2027, more units come under regulation ([Province of Manitoba](https://news.gov.mb.ca/news/?archive=&item=75138)). Buildings first occupied after March 7, 2005 are exempt for 20 years, so newly built competitors sit outside the guideline.

Owners who complete major capital work can apply for an [above-guideline increase](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/landlord/aboveguide.html), but approval depends on documented costs. A planned program with itemized scopes can make that process simpler.

Those applications now recover less. [On October 30, 2026](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/regs/annual/2026/116.php), Manitoba's regulation cut each capital share by 40%, leaving 20%, 15%, 10% or 7.5% of the cost by item. And since October 20, 2026, tenants have not had to pay any of a proposed increase before the Branch's order.
Claims are limited to costs already paid or billed, with any rebates listed.

A rehabilitation scheme is a separate route. It needs the Branch's approval, the rules limit work done before the first order, and an approved scheme can exempt a complex or part of one for up to 5 years, or a single unit for up to 2 years.
Questions to ask before you start

Before committing to a multi-year program, owners and property managers should be able to answer a few questions. How long do you plan to hold the building? A five-year hold justifies different work than a 15-year hold.

What is your current turnover rate, and why do tenants leave? Exit surveys and maintenance logs often reveal the answer. Which nearby new buildings are you competing with, and what do they offer at what rent? And what is your realistic budget per year, including reserves for emergencies?
Answering those questions turns a renovation wish list into a plan with priorities and a schedule.
The bottom line

Winnipeg's building boom is a sign of a growing city, and older buildings can still compete. They will not win on newness, but they can win on location, character, value and condition. A planned renovation program protects the asset, helps keep tenants and positions the building for a market with more choice.
